guides/python-checks.title: Check Python linting and types together

execution.scope: Windows with Python 3.13.15, Ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2; selected findings in faulty and corrected examples. Other hosts were not executed.

sources.label: Ruff rule selection and exit behavior

guides/python-checks.markdown: # Check Python linting and types together [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) and [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) answer different questions. This recipe gives both the same fixture: an unused import and a call that passes text to an integer parameter. Ruff checks only `F401`; mypy checks the annotated call. Neither runs the target program. Start with [Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/) to download or clone the repository. From the downloaded repository's root, enter the fixture directory: ```powershell Set-Location examples/python-checks ``` [`examples/python-checks`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/python-checks) contains `bad/greeting.py`, the corrected `good/greeting.py`, a shared `pyproject.toml`, pinned requirements, and `run_checks.py`. **Executed on Windows with Python 3.13.15.** Both expected findings appeared in the faulty file and both checks were clean on the corrected file. The [execution record and reports](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/python-checks/evidence.md) retain the environment and tested input hashes. Other hosts have not been run for this recipe. ## Prepare an isolated environment Use Python 3.13 and the pinned Ruff 0.14.3 and mypy 1.18.2 releases. These versions are a reproducible example, not a recommendation to downgrade an existing project. The target Python version is also set to 3.13 in `pyproject.toml`. On Windows, select an interpreter and check it before creating the environment: ```powershell $Python = "python" & $Python --version ``` Expect `Python 3.13.x`. If that command is missing or reports another version, set `$Python` to your Python 3.13 executable, such as `$Python = "C:\path\to\Python313\python.exe"`, and repeat the check. Continue from `examples/python-checks` once the version matches: ```powershell & $Python -m venv .venv .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install -r requirements.txt ``` On Linux or macOS, use `.venv/bin/python` in place of the Windows interpreter path. Installing the pinned packages requires package-index access. The fixture has no application dependencies or service credentials. ## Check the faulty version Run both checks and keep their reports: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py bad --output reports/bad ``` The runner verifies versions, runs each tool separately, and saves commands, input hashes, host details, versions, and return codes in `run.json`. Diagnostics go in `ruff.json` and `mypy.txt`, with separate stderr files. Read both reports. Use a new output directory for each rerun; the runner refuses to overwrite earlier reports. It records setup failures and retains partial output on timeout. The expected signals are: | Tool | Expected finding | Meaning | | ---- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | | Ruff | `F401` for `math` | The imported module is unused. | | mypy | `arg-type` at `greeting("three")` | The argument is text, but the parameter is annotated as an integer. | The runner returns `1` when the checks complete with findings, `0` when both complete without findings, and `2` when either cannot complete. These are this runner's gate rules, not universal analyzer exit codes. Tool completion is recorded separately from the gate in `run.json`. ## Check the correction The corrected file removes the unused import and calls `greeting(3)`. Run the same configuration against it: ```powershell .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe run_checks.py good --output reports/good ``` Both reports should be clean for this fixture. The known defects and correction show that the selected checks are active. They do not measure general defect coverage or prove that the program meets every requirement. ## Use it on your project `run_checks.py` accepts only `bad` and `good`; it is a demonstration runner. For your code, run the tools directly. From `examples/python-checks`, keep the checker interpreter's absolute path, then enter your project's root: ```powershell $CheckPython = (Resolve-Path .\.venv\Scripts\python.exe).Path Set-Location "C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT" ``` Replace `C:\path\to\YOUR_PROJECT` with your project directory. Use its existing analyzer configuration. If it has none, add these tables to its root `pyproject.toml`, creating the file only if absent. Merge settings into any existing tables instead of replacing the file: ```toml [tool.ruff] target-version = "py313" [tool.ruff.lint] select = ["E4", "E7", "E9", "F"] [tool.mypy] python_version = "3.13" strict = true show_error_codes = true pretty = false ``` Match both target-version settings to the Python version your project supports. The fixture selects only `F401`; this starting selection adds other Pyflakes and selected pycodestyle checks. Review the [Ruff configuration](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/configuration/) for your project. If your settings live in `ruff.toml` or `mypy.ini`, use those paths in the corresponding config arguments below. The checker environment needs access to your project's dependencies and type stubs. Install the project's declared dependencies and needed stub packages in that environment, or use a project environment with the checkers installed by setting `$CheckPython` to its interpreter. Resolve [missing imports and stubs](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html#missing-imports) before treating a clean result as useful type coverage. Choose one small source directory and a new report directory for this run: ```powershell $Target = ".\src\YOUR_PACKAGE" $Reports = ".\check-reports\first-run" New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path $Reports -ErrorAction Stop | Out-Null & $CheckPython -m ruff check --no-fix --no-cache --config pyproject.toml ` --output-format json $Target > "$Reports\ruff.json" 2> "$Reports\ruff.stderr.txt" $RuffExit = $LASTEXITCODE $RuffExit | Set-Content "$Reports\ruff.exit.txt" & $CheckPython -m mypy --no-incremental --cache-dir "$Reports\mypy-cache" ` --config-file pyproject.toml $Target > "$Reports\mypy.txt" 2> "$Reports\mypy.stderr.txt" $MypyExit = $LASTEXITCODE $MypyExit | Set-Content "$Reports\mypy.exit.txt" ``` Replace `src\YOUR_PACKAGE` with the directory you want checked. Use a different `$Reports` path for every run; stop if directory creation fails. These commands make no automatic source fixes. Read `ruff.json`, `mypy.txt`, and both stderr files with their separate exit codes. Ruff returns `0` for no findings, `1` for findings, and `2` for a failed run. A completed mypy run reports either success or a diagnostic summary; an empty report or a setup error is not a clean result. Review and correct findings, then repeat with a new report directory. Record the source revision, selected configuration, exclusions, and environment using the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Keep diagnostics separate; do not compare raw issue counts as measures of quality. Use the [CI result-handling guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) to decide which completed findings block a change and how to retain failed or incomplete runs. ## Sources - [Python virtual environments](https://docs.python.org/3.13/library/venv.html) - [Ruff rule selection and exit behavior](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/linter/) - [Ruff 0.14.3 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/ruff/0.14.3/) - [mypy 1.18.2 distribution](https://pypi.org/project/mypy/1.18.2/) - [mypy file and import scope](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html)

# Get the examples

Use this snapshot for the Python, API, and Windows memory walkthroughs. It
contains the example files; each walkthrough explains which tools to install.

## Download the snapshot

[Download the example snapshot (ZIP)](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/archive/506c522ca86fd8c9d7b688f35a4d37f842d04cc9.zip)
and extract it, or run these commands in PowerShell from an empty working
directory:

```powershell
Invoke-WebRequest 'https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/archive/506c522ca86fd8c9d7b688f35a4d37f842d04cc9.zip' -OutFile examples.zip
Expand-Archive -LiteralPath examples.zip -DestinationPath .
Set-Location '.\ToolWiki-506c522ca86fd8c9d7b688f35a4d37f842d04cc9'
```

You are now at the repository root: the directory containing `README.md` and
`examples`. If you extracted the ZIP elsewhere, open that directory instead.

| Walkthrough                                                                              | Working directory from the repository root |
| ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| [Python linting and types](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/)    | `Set-Location examples/python-checks`      |
| [Disposable HTTP API](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/)           | Stay at the repository root.               |
| [Windows memory check](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/) | `Set-Location examples/windows-memory`     |

## Use Git instead

Clone into a new directory and select the same snapshot:

```powershell
git clone https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki.git ToolWiki-examples
Set-Location ToolWiki-examples
git checkout --detach 506c522ca86fd8c9d7b688f35a4d37f842d04cc9
```

The [snapshot revision](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/commit/506c522ca86fd8c9d7b688f35a4d37f842d04cc9)
keeps the examples stable while the wiki changes. Keep your reports outside a
fresh checkout or in the output directories named by the walkthrough.

tools/ruff.markdown: # Ruff ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed in this review.** [Install Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/installation/), then save this as `sample.py`: ```python import math print("Ready") ``` Run this in the directory containing the file. It checks for unused imports without changing the file or loading project configuration: ```sh ruff check --isolated --select F401 sample.py ``` Representative diagnostic excerpt, not captured output (formatting varies by version): ```text sample.py:1:8: F401 `math` imported but unused ``` The location identifies the import; `F401` identifies the unused-import rule. Remove that line and repeat the check. A clean result means this selected rule found no violation in this file. ## Use it on your project Follow the [Ruff tutorial](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/tutorial/) to configure rule selection, file exclusions, and the target Python version. Run `ruff check` for linting; `ruff format` only formats code. Start without automatic fixes so you can inspect the diagnostics. ## Fixes and limitations Ruff distinguishes safe and unsafe fixes. Review proposed changes and run your tests after applying them. Record the tool version, configuration, and preview setting for repeatable results. ## Alternatives and complements Follow the [Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) to check one project with separate lint and type reports. Pair Ruff with [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) or [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) when you also need type checking. Consider [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) for a dedicated Python security-rule workflow. [Pylint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pylint/) uses inference and supports plugins; Ruff provides built-in rule families. Their rules overlap but are not interchangeable. Before switching, compare the diagnostics and plugin requirements of your project. The [official comparison](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/faq/#how-does-ruffs-linter-compare-to-pylint) explains these differences. Use the [finding review workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) to investigate a diagnostic and verify a correction.

tools/mypy.markdown: # mypy ## Where it fits Use mypy to check whether code uses the types described by annotations and stubs consistently. It complements [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) for linting and [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) for selected Python security patterns. A clean lint run is not a type-checking result. Gradual typing lets a project adopt annotations in stages. By default, bodies of functions without annotations receive limited checking. `Any` and ignored imports can also let type mistakes pass unnoticed. ## First try **Illustrative example, not run here.** Follow the [mypy installation instructions](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started.html) in your selected Python environment, then save this as `sample.py`: ```python def next_count(count: int) -> int: return count + 1 next_count("three") ``` Check it without running the program: ```sh python -m mypy sample.py ``` Representative diagnostic, not captured output (formatting varies by version): ```text sample.py:4: error: Argument 1 to "next_count" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int" [arg-type] ``` `sample.py:4` locates the call. `arg-type` identifies an incompatible argument type: text was passed to an integer parameter. Replace the argument with `3` and check again. This example exercises one mismatch, not the entire type system. See the [argument-type diagnostic reference](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/error_code_list.html#check-argument-types-arg-type) for details. Use the [shared Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) for a pinned environment, faulty/corrected files, and separate reports. ## Configure a useful check Supply the project's imports and any required third-party stubs. Start with a small annotated area, inspect errors, and tighten the configuration deliberately. `--check-untyped-defs` can inspect unannotated bodies, while `--strict` enables a broader set of checks. Record the mypy version, configuration, target Python version, and suppressions. Static types do not validate arbitrary input data at runtime or replace application tests. [Compare mypy, Ruff, and Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fmypy%2Ctools%2Fruff%2Ctools%2Fbandit) to see their different roles. ## Compare Python type checkers [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) is another Python type checker. Both use annotations and stubs, but configuration, inference, diagnostics, and plugin support differ. For a useful trial, check the same revision with matching Python version, platform, imports, and intended strictness. Investigate disagreements instead of comparing diagnostic counts. Keep [mypy import and stub settings](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html) and [Pyright settings](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) with the reports. [Compare mypy and Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fmypy%2Ctools%2Fpyright). Ruff remains complementary for lint rules; running two type checkers is a deliberate evaluation choice, not a requirement of the Python recipe.
